sections.title: Master of Bioethics Capstone Seminar
sections.description: This semester-long seminar serves a culminating research experience in the MBE program and is open to all MBE students. In this seminar, students propose a topic for original, independent research and produce a piece of scholarly work with guidance from the course instructor and capstone classmates. Students attend a biweekly seminar while completing their projects to learn research skills and workshop their project with their peers. Students also have one-on-one capstone meetings with the course instructor. The course concludes with a Capstone project event, during which each participant presents their work. This course is only open to students in the Master of Bioethics program. Students must propose a tentative research topic before registering for the course.

sections.title: Master of Bioethics Capstone Seminar
sections.description: This semester-long seminar serves as a culminating research experience in the MBE program and is open to all MBE students. In this seminar, students work on their own original research project with guidance from the course instructor and capstone classmates. Students attend a biweekly seminar while completing their projects to learn research skills and workshop their project with their peers. Students choose the final product of their research, including conference or poster presentations, ethical guidance for an organization, research papers, and an even solo or co-authored published academic articles. This course is only open to students in the Master of Bioethics program. Students must propose a tentative research topic before registering for the course. Examples of published past Capstones include: Attiah, M. A. (2013). Treat Me Like a Child. Jama, 310(7). Hrycko, A. J., & Sinderbrand, M. (2025). Inpatient Hospitalization of Adolescents Diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder: An Ethical Analysis. The American Journal of Bioethics, 1-7. Yerramilli, D. (2014). On cultivating the courage to speak up: the critical role of attendings in the moral development of physicians in training. Hastings Center Report, 44(5), 30-32.
